extracted.intended_audience: university teachers, Catholic educators, clergy, and educated public interested in the philosophy of education
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of what constitutes a University (especially a Catholic University), the Church's duties toward liberal knowledge, and the ethical consequences of philosophical versus religious modes of culture. Combines prescriptive standards about institutional governance with normative criteria for character and curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical religion presents partial truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no doctrine contained in them which is not in a certain sense true; yet, on the other hand, that almost every statement is perverted and made false, because it is not the whole truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical/external renderings of religion exhibit truth only under one aspect and so are insufficient: they may state something true but, by omitting the rest of the truth, distort its moral force (e.g., treating conscience as merely an "irrational" pang or virtue as mere taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral judgement must not be confined to outward beauty or fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: “It has no better measure of right and wrong than that of visible beauty and tangible fitness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against measuring virtue by appearance, utility, or social decorum. If conscience and interior moral depth are dismissed, ethics degenerates into what merely pleases or avoids offence; detection and scandal replace actual moral assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual refinement can excuse vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Refined intellectual civilization may begin by repelling sensuality but end by excusing it; detection, not the sin, becomes the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions that social prestige, taste, and aesthetic refinement can cover or legitimize immoral conduct (illustrated by Burke's phrase: "vice lost half its evil by losing all its grossness"). Assessment of morality must look beneath refinement and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: True religion is rooted and formative; intellectual counterfeits are shallow
rubrics_metrics.description: “True Religion is slow in growth, and, when once planted, is difficult of dislodgement; but its intellectual counterfeit has no root in itself: it springs up suddenly, it suddenly withers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious formation by its depth and durability: authentic religious education aims at inner regeneration; mere philosophical religion aims at exterior decorum and is liable to wither when pressures change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical morality is ornamental not regenerative
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy often aims only at present life and external accomplishments—"like teaching them a language or an accomplishment"—rather than at moral conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral curricula or ethical systems, distinguish between trainings that cultivate external behaviour and those that seek inner transformation; the latter are the Church's primary concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between humility and modesty (tests of virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility is an inward abdication of privilege and a placing of oneself in the position of inferiors; modesty is primarily outward deportment and may be compatible with pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate modesty (a social demeanor) with true humility (a moral and theological virtue). Assessments of character should look for inward disposition and tests that reveal delicate, subtle self-abasement rather than mere external restraint or polished manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and qualities of a gentleman (ethical character formed by cultivated intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman 'never inflicts pain' — he removes obstacles to others, avoids causing offence, is tender to the bashful, merciful to the absurd, discreet in conversation, brief and decisive, respectful of religion, tolerant, and refrains from malice and vindictiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this catalogue of dispositions and behaviours as criteria for judging cultivated social character: attentiveness to others' ease, moderation in speech, courtesy, patience, forbearance, and respect for institutions (including religion) indicate the civilized ethical ideal described.

rubrics_metrics.name: A University must teach Catholic theology to be truly Catholic
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the Catholic Faith is true, a University cannot exist externally to the Catholic pale, for it cannot teach Universal Knowledge if it does not teach Catholic theology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an institution to claim the title 'Catholic University' it must include Catholic theology within its curriculum in a way that makes theological truth integral to the University's account of universal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church jurisdiction and spiritual spirit are necessary for Catholic character of an institution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient that Catholic theology be professed; the Church must "breathe her own pure and unearthly spirit into it, and fashion and mould its organization, and watch over its teaching, and knit together its pupils, and superintend its action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional Catholicity by governance, organizational spirit, pastoral supervision, and active oversight — not merely by the presence of theological chairs or formal professions of doctrine. Example: the Spanish Inquisition was materially Catholic but lacked the Church's proper character because it was a State institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary dangers from Liberal Knowledge to Revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: First: simple ignoring of Theological Truth; second: recognition but adulteration of the spirit of Revelation (i.e., accepting Catholicism in form while recasting its spirit by earthly standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating university curricula or scholarly practice, check whether liberal studies lead to (a) exclusion of theology from the intellectual domain or (b) assimilation/corruption of revelation by philosophical standards (resulting in indifference, laxity, or heresy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct effects of Science and Literature on religion; keep theological and physical inquiries distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Human reason investigates God, Nature, and Man; Literature and Science make up Liberal Education. "Science is made to subserve the former of the two injuries, which Revealed Truth sustains—its exclusion; Literature subserves the latter—its corruption." Also: as Bacon argued, from religious investigations, as such, physics must be excluded, and from physical, as such, religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate disciplines by their different tendencies: physical science tends (in practice) to marginalize theological claims if allowed to encroach, while literature/philosophical study tends to re-cast or dilute theological spirit. Preserve methodological boundaries: do not mix theological questions with empirical physical inquiry in ways that spoil each domain.
